desc:
You hold a string s and may only change it at its right end. One move is either

  • remove the last character, or
  • append any lowercase letter to the end.

Return the minimum number of moves that turn s into t. Removing everything and typing t from scratch always works, so an answer exists. Either string may be empty.

s = "abcde", t = "abxy"  ->  5   (remove e, d, c, then append x, y)
s = "same",  t = "same"  ->  0
s = "",      t = "ab"    ->  2
s = "xyz",   t = "abc"   ->  6
constraints: Both strings contain only lowercase English letters
hints: Characters in the middle of the string can never be touched without first removing everything after them. So which part of s can survive unchanged?
The surviving part is a prefix of s that is also a prefix of t. Keeping a longer one is always better, so look at the longest common prefix.
If the longest common prefix has length L, you remove len(s) - L characters and then append len(t) - L characters.
editorial: Because moves only affect the last character, a character at position i of s stays untouched only if nothing at or before the moment of its removal reaches it, which means the final string must start with the same prefix. So the surviving part is a common prefix of s and t. Every character of s beyond it must be removed, and every character of t beyond it must be appended.

A longer surviving prefix saves moves on both sides, so take the longest common prefix of length L. The answer is (len(s) - L) + (len(t) - L). This is the simplest member of the edit distance family: the only 'alignment' possible is prefix against prefix, so no table is needed. The full edit distance later relaxes exactly this restriction.
